claims.text: The untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy has hierarchical dual-phase lamellar colonies and limited room-temperature tensile ductility.
Dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries cause local stress concentrations, microcracking, and brittle failure in the untreated alloy.
Severe plastic deformation followed by optimized annealing can refine the lamellar spacing and create an interconnected nanolamellar substructure.
Reduced and more uniform lamellar spacing facilitates continuous dislocation transmission across phase boundaries.
Frequent lamellar barriers created by spacing refinement promote dislocation cross-boundary transmission.
Cross-boundary dislocation transmission reduces localized dislocation pile-ups.
Transmission and shearing across lamellar boundaries alleviate local stress concentrations.
Alleviating boundary stress concentrations mitigates microcrack nucleation and propagation during tensile straining.
The nanolamellar modification will increase room-temperature tensile strain-to-failure relative to the untreated alloy.
The nanolamellar modification will maintain or slightly increase yield strength and ultimate tensile strength.
Concurrent improvement in strength and ductility is possible in a refractory high-entropy alloy through microstructural modification.
The proposed effect applies under room-temperature tensile loading.
The intervention requires reliable production of a uniformly nanolamellar architecture.
Excessive grain coarsening or formation of deleterious phases may limit the intervention's efficacy.
Performance under high-temperature or cyclic loading is not established.
The optimal degree of lamellar refinement and the quantitative strength and ductility improvements depend on processing parameters and alloy composition.
